A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpurLens research despite the changed title and formatting. The text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original perception and hallucination experiments, prompting and token-dropping ablations, and vision-encoder classifier experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds human validation, CelebA and Waterbirds evaluations, and further component and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: The GPT-4 proposal, OWLv2 ranking, and top/bottom-K gap pipeline remains. v2 extends the reported screening procedure with six detector-oriented filtering checks in Appendix A and introduces a dataset-adequacy procedure in Appendix P. Appendix N still mentions manual review, so its removal is not established.

E1.justification: The original ImageNet, HardImageNet, COCO, and Spurious ImageNet coverage is retained. Appendices G–H add CelebA blond-hair recognition across gender groups and Waterbirds recognition across bird/background combinations, substantially broadening the represented tasks and input conditions.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds Spurious List and Spurious Top prompting comparators. Appendix E compares GPT-4 cue proposals with Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen2.5 72B; Appendix O adds YOLO World and quantitative comparisons with GroundingDINO, which v1 already discussed qualitatively. The original ranking and random baselines remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces human-validation protocols using top/bottom-10 images from 20 COCO and 25 ImageNet classes, plus 20 COCO object-cue pairs evaluated at K=50. It also adds proposal-similarity thresholds, group-specific benchmark prompts, and a vision-encoder comparison using f=7, K=50, and maximal available training data. These extend the evaluation design; the earlier classifier sampling sweep and principal benchmark settings remain.

E4.justification: New analyses examine proposal-model consistency, human alignment, sensitivity to K, alternative detectors, dataset adequacy, and cue-aware prompting. Appendix M adds a direct comparison of vision-only and full-model gaps. Conversely, v1's cross-model normalized-gap heatmap and accompanying analysis are removed. Earlier token-dropping, masking, and classifier ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit correlation and regression estimation, including Pearson correlation for human alignment in Figure 11 and fitted lines with R-squared values in Figure 20. The existing 10 classifier repetitions and 16-by-16 random-ranking baseline procedure remain unchanged; no new confidence intervals or seed listings are provided.

E6.justification: Many aggregate scores and class-wise cue/result entries change. For example, GPT-4o-mini's COCO perception scores in Table 1 change from 87.6/69.7 to 88.0/67.6, with the gap increasing from 17.9 to 20.4 points. v2 also reports new human agreement results of 92.5% on COCO and 89.4% on ImageNet, plus new benchmark and robustness findings. Revised cue screening and selection prevent interpreting the updated gaps as matched-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The PA/HR definitions and Appendix B probability derivations are retained. Appendix E introduces the thresholded proposal-similarity definition, and Appendix P formalizes a dataset-adequacy criterion based on sufficiently represented cues and feasible K values. These are limited mathematical additions, without new proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims about automated, interpretable cue discovery and the two MLLM failure modes remain. However, v2 drops the conclusion's claim that biases likely originate within the vision encoder and explicitly limits SpurLens to diagnosis without identifying root causes or robust mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive boundaries concerning precision versus completeness, direct comparisons between models, dataset diversity, runtime, and causal interpretation. It qualifies the relevance of CelebA and Waterbirds and acknowledges information leakage in Spurious Top prompting. Appendix M adds a partial-attribution interpretation based on a 0.25 correlation, although stronger earlier attribution language remains elsewhere in that appendix.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands exact filtering instructions and supplies two additional mitigation prompts. New appendices specify embedding models, thresholds, human-validation sample sizes, and additional evaluation procedures. A reproducibility statement reports supplementary code submission and a planned public release, without providing a public repository link. Conversely, v1's explicit instruction to randomize zero-score ties is omitted.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning against interpretable bias-discovery work by Eyuboglu, Zhang, and Wiles, distinguishing their annotation, human-selection, or synthetic-data requirements. Additional references support CelebA, YOLO World, and caption-based discovery. The main positioning against spuriosity rankings and hallucination benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: The title changes to emphasize SpurLens, several passages are condensed or rewritten, and Section 5.2 becomes Object Hallucination. Prompt documentation gains subsections, mitigation discussion moves partly to Appendix J, and class-wise results are consolidated under Appendix S. Much of the original prose and the main-section sequence remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. The fire-hydrant diagram is rearranged, separate PA/HR plots are merged, the cross-model heatmap is removed, and the hallucination gallery is split. Table 4 is transposed and expanded. Numerous new validation tables, scatterplots, sensitivity curves, and detector examples substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 relied mainly on qualitative detector inspection and ranking-baseline comparisons to validate SpurLens. v2 adds quantitative human agreement and human-derived gap comparisons, addressing an important weakness in establishing whether detector-generated rankings are meaningful. Component checks, sensitivity analysis, and clearer applicability limits further strengthen the paper. Inconsistencies about manual review and vision-encoder attribution remain, but the added validation and more careful claim boundaries provide a substantial overall improvement.
